13400:
Recognize means to encounter something and know it from before. Your mind makes a connection: "I know this. I've experienced this before."

This is the thread that runs through almost all uses of the word — a meeting between what's in front of you right now and knowledge you already hold.

1. To identify someone or something from memory

This is the most everyday use. You see, hear, smell, or otherwise sense something, and your brain immediately places it — connects it to something stored in your memory.

  • She recognized her old teacher's handwriting on the envelope.
  • He recognized the song the moment it started playing.
  • I recognized the smell of rain before I even looked out the window.
  • The dog recognized its owner's footsteps on the stairs.

The crucial point here: you can only recognize something you already know. If you've never seen a particular face before, you cannot recognize it. This is what distinguishes "recognize" from "notice." Noticing means you become aware of something. Recognizing means you identify it through prior knowledge. You can notice a stranger, but you cannot recognize one.

2. To acknowledge or accept that something is true

Here, "recognize" shifts from identification toward acceptance. You consciously admit or accept a fact — especially one that is important, difficult, or inconvenient.

  • The manager recognized that the plan had failed.
  • We must recognize that change won't happen overnight.
  • She recognized her own mistake before anyone pointed it out.
  • It's important to recognize the limits of what we know.

In this meaning, "recognize" is close to "acknowledge" or "admit," but it carries a more deliberate, thoughtful tone. When you recognize a truth, you're not just passively knowing it — you're actively accepting it.

3. To officially honor someone's effort or achievement

Organizations, institutions, and authorities "recognize" people or their work as a form of formal appreciation and credit.

  • The university recognized her decades of service with an honorary degree.
  • The team was publicly recognized for its outstanding work.
  • The award recognizes individuals who have made exceptional contributions to science.

Here, "recognize" means: we see what you've done, we acknowledge it, and we're giving it the attention it deserves.

4. To formally and officially acknowledge the existence or legitimacy of something

In law, diplomacy, and formal institutions, "recognize" means to accept something as valid and legitimate — to officially treat it as real.

  • Dozens of countries recognized the new government after the elections.
  • The court refused to recognize the agreement as legally binding.
  • The organization was formally recognized by the international body.
  • The state does not recognize same-sex marriage.

This is "recognize" in its most serious, institutional form. When a government recognizes another country, it is declaring: "We accept that you exist and have the standing you claim." Withholding recognition, in international law, is itself a powerful act.

This phrase deserves its own spotlight because it's extremely common and useful.

"Recognized as" means to be widely accepted or acknowledged as being a particular thing — usually something of significance.

  • Einstein is recognized as one of the greatest scientific minds in history.
  • She is recognized as the foremost expert in her field.
  • The painting was recognized as a forgery.
  • This region is recognized as the birthplace of modern jazz.

The phrase implies that there is broad agreement or official acknowledgment about what something is or what category it belongs to.

Recognize vs. Notice
Noticing is simply becoming aware of something — you can notice something you've never seen before.
Recognizing requires prior knowledge. You recognize what you already know.

  • You noticed the stranger who walked in. You recognized your old friend.

Recognize vs. Remember
Remembering is bringing something back from memory on your own — your mind generates the thought without an external trigger.
Recognizing is triggered by something in front of you — a person, a place, a sound — that activates the memory.

  • You remember your friend's name when someone asks.
  • You recognize your friend when you spot their face in a crowd.

Recognize vs. Know
Knowing is having information about something in general.
Recognizing is the active moment of identification — matching what's in front of you to what's in your memory.

  • You know that the Eiffel Tower is in Paris.
  • When you see it in person for the first time, you recognize it from all the photos you've seen.

Understanding how a word behaves in a sentence is part of truly knowing it.

Recognize + object (direct identification)
→ "I recognized his voice immediately."

Recognize + that + clause (acknowledging a truth)
→ "She recognized that the situation was serious."

Recognize + someone/something + as + noun (identifying what category something is)
→ "They recognized him as the rightful owner."
→ "The disease was recognized as a public health emergency."

Recognize + someone + for + something (honoring)
→ "She was recognized for her bravery."

Fail to recognize / not recognize (common negation)
→ "He had aged so much that I almost didn't recognize him."
→ "The law fails to recognize this type of agreement."

When you say you recognize something, it usually implies a fairly confident identification. But it's not always absolute. People can think they recognize a face and be wrong. That's why eyewitness identification — "I recognize this person" — can be unreliable in law. The feeling of recognition can sometimes be misleading.

There's even a specific term for the eerie feeling of recognizing something you shouldn't recognize: déjà vu — a sense of false recognition, where something unfamiliar feels strangely familiar.

In formal meetings and legislative bodies, "recognize" has a very specific meaning: to formally give someone permission to speak.

  • "The chair recognizes the senator from Delhi."

This is the presiding officer officially acknowledging that a particular person now has the floor to speak. It's rare outside of formal proceedings, but worth knowing.

The word "recognize" does a lot of work, but all its meanings share a common backbone: bringing something to conscious awareness and giving it a name, a place, or a status. Whether you're identifying a face, admitting a difficult truth, honoring someone's work, or formally accepting a government's legitimacy — you are in each case taking something and saying: "I see what this is, and I am acknowledging it."

That acknowledgment can be private and instant (recognizing a smell), or public and formal (recognizing a country), but the spirit is the same.
13401:
To recoil means to suddenly move backward or pull away — either physically or emotionally — as a powerful reaction to something. Think of it as your body or mind saying "No — away from this, right now" in a sharp, instinctive burst.

The key ingredients are always there: something happens → and in response, something snaps, jerks, or pulls sharply backward. It is never a slow, calm retreat. It is a sudden, reactive withdrawal driven by force, fear, or disgust.

1. The Physical Meaning — something springs or jerks backward

This is about real, literal movement. When a force acts on something and causes it to snap sharply in the opposite direction, that thing recoils.

The most classic example is a gun. When a gun fires, the explosion of energy inside drives the bullet forward — but that same energy pushes the gun backward into the shooter's hand or shoulder. That backward kick is called recoil. The gun literally springs back against you.

A spring works the same way. Compress it tightly, then release it — it doesn't ease out slowly. It recoils — snapping back with force to its original shape.

Other examples:

  • The cannon recoiled violently after the shot.
  • The branch recoiled and whipped back into place after he let go of it.

Notice the pattern: something was under pressure or force → it was released or triggered → it snapped sharply backward. That's physical recoil.

2. The Emotional/Psychological Meaning — to shrink back in fear, disgust, or horror

This is the more commonly used meaning in everyday English. Here, a person recoils when something so disturbing, frightening, or repulsive happens that their body or mind instinctively pulls away from it.

This can be:

  • A physical, visible reaction — your body actually jerks backward, you step back, your face scrunches up, you draw your hands close — all without even consciously deciding to do so.
  • A mental/emotional reaction — your mind pulls away from an idea, a memory, a thought, or a suggestion, refusing to engage with it.

Examples:

  • She recoiled when she saw the spider on her pillow.
  • He recoiled at the smell coming from the garbage bin.
  • The child recoiled in horror as the villain appeared on screen.
  • She recoiled from the idea of eating raw meat.
  • He recoiled at the suggestion that he had cheated.

In each case, something unpleasant, shocking, or threatening triggered a rapid, instinctive pulling-away reaction. The person didn't think about it — they recoiled. It was automatic.

Both the physical and emotional meanings share the same underlying idea: a sharp, reactive backward movement caused by something external.

In the gun: the explosion causes the gun to snap back.
In the person: the spider (or smell, or horror) causes the person to snap back.

It is always:

  • Sudden — not gradual
  • Reactive — triggered by something outside you
  • Backward or away — a withdrawal, not a forward motion
  • Forceful or instinctive — not a gentle, calm step back

Recoil is almost always triggered by one of these:

  • Fear — He recoiled when the dog snapped at him.
  • Disgust or revulsion — She recoiled at the sight of the wound.
  • Shock or horror — The crowd recoiled in disbelief.
  • Strong moral rejection — He recoiled from the cruelty he witnessed.
  • Pain or anticipated pain — She recoiled as the needle came close.
  • Physical force (in the literal sense) — The rifle recoiled against his shoulder.
The Emotional Weight of the Word

Recoil is not a neutral word. It carries a strong emotional charge. When you say someone recoiled, you are communicating that their reaction was intense and visceral — not mild or polite.

Compare:

  • She stepped back from the crowd. — calm, deliberate
  • She moved away from the idea. — gentle, logical
  • She recoiled from the crowd / the idea. — strong, instinctive, almost involuntary

Recoil tells your reader: this wasn't a gentle disagreement or a quiet discomfort. This was a gut-level, deeply felt pulling away.
How Recoil Compares to Similar Words

Flinch — a small, quick, involuntary movement, usually in anticipation of pain. Flinching is smaller and more contained. He flinched when she raised her hand. Recoil is stronger and more whole-body.

Wince — similar to flinch, but often just a facial tightening in response to pain or embarrassment. She winced at the loud noise. It's mostly facial. Recoil involves more of you.

Shrink back — to slowly, gradually draw back. Shrinking back implies something more creeping and sustained. Recoiling is faster and sharper.

Recoil is the strongest of these — the most forceful, the most dramatic, and the most involuntary-feeling.

Recoil is typically followed by specific prepositions:

  • Recoil FROM something — the most common pattern. You recoil from whatever is causing the reaction.
    She recoiled from the flames.
  • Recoil AT something — you recoil at a sight, smell, thought, or suggestion.
    He recoiled at the idea.
  • Recoil IN something — usually used with words like horror, disgust, shock, fear.
    They recoiled in horror.
Intensity — How Strong Is This Word?

Recoil is a strong, vivid, expressive word. It belongs to a register of words that describe sharp, involuntary, dramatic reactions. Writers use it to make a scene feel visceral and immediate. If someone recoils in your story, your reader will feel the intensity of the moment.

It is not a word you'd use for mild discomfort. You don't recoil from a slightly bitter cup of tea or a movie you mildly disliked. You recoil from something that genuinely shocks, repulses, or frightens you.

To recoil means to suddenly and sharply spring back or pull away — either physically (like a gun snapping backward after firing) or emotionally (like a person jerking back instinctively in fear, disgust, or horror).
13402:
To recollect means to remember something, especially by making a conscious, deliberate effort to bring it back to mind from your memory.

The key idea here is effort. When you recollect something, you are not passively receiving a memory that floats up on its own — you are actively reaching back into your mind and searching for it. Think of your memory as a vast storage room. To recollect is to walk into that room and deliberately look for something.
The Feeling of Effort Inside the Word

This is the most important thing to understand about "recollect."

When you remember something, it can happen effortlessly — a smell might suddenly make you remember your grandmother's kitchen. No searching required.

But when you recollect something, there is usually a sense that you are trying — sometimes straining — to retrieve a memory that is not immediately clear or obvious. The memory might be distant, faint, or buried under time. You pause, think, and pull it back.

This is why "recollect" is very often used:

  • when someone is unsure whether they can remember something
  • when someone is reflecting on the past carefully
  • when the memory in question is old or not easily accessible

"I'm trying to recollect where I've seen her before."

Here, the speaker is clearly making a mental effort — it's not an instant memory.
How It Differs From Similar Words

Remember, recall, and recollect are close in meaning, but they carry slightly different shades.

  • Remember is the most general and everyday word. It covers both effortless and effortful memories. You can use it in almost any situation.
  • Recall is similar to recollect — it also suggests deliberate retrieval. However, "recall" often feels more sharp and precise, like pulling up specific facts or details quickly. It can also feel slightly more formal.
  • Recollect carries the most sense of slow, thoughtful, reflective remembering. It is the word you would use when you are sitting quietly and carefully searching your memory, especially for past events or experiences. It has a slightly old-fashioned, literary quality compared to "recall."

Think of it this way:

  • "I can't remember his name." — plain, everyday, neutral
  • "I can't recall his name." — slightly more deliberate, formal
  • "I can't quite recollect his name." — reflective, searching, slightly more formal or literary
How to Use It in a Sentence (Grammar)

Recollect is a transitive verb, meaning it typically takes an object — something that is being remembered. Here are the most common sentence patterns:

1. Recollect + noun (a thing/person/event)

"She could not recollect the exact date."
"I recollect that summer very well."

2. Recollect + that + clause

"I recollect that he was quite nervous during the meeting."
"She recollected that the door had been left open."

3. Recollect + -ing (a past action)

"I don't recollect seeing him at the party."
"He recollected hearing a strange noise that night."

4. Recollect + question word (where/when/who/what/how)

"Can you recollect where you put your passport?"
"I can't recollect when we first met."

Recollect sits on the more formal and literary end of the spectrum. You are more likely to encounter it in:

  • literary fiction and older novels
  • formal or careful speech
  • courtroom or official testimony ("As far as I can recollect...")
  • thoughtful essays or memoirs

In everyday casual conversation, most people would simply say "remember" instead. If someone said "I don't recollect" in a casual chat with a friend, it might sound a little stiff or old-fashioned — though perfectly correct.

These examples will show you the word in action across different situations:

"The old man sat quietly, trying to recollect the name of the street where he had grown up."

— A slow, reflective effort to retrieve an old memory.

"I vaguely recollect meeting her at a conference, but I'm not entirely sure."

— The memory is uncertain and incomplete — classic territory for "recollect."

"Do you recollect what time the train was supposed to arrive?"

— A question asking someone to make an effort to remember.

"She recollected, with a sharp pang, the last conversation she had with her father."

— Bringing a meaningful past memory deliberately to mind.

"As far as I can recollect, no one mentioned anything about a change in plans."

— A very common formal phrase, signaling that the speaker is offering their best memory, not absolute certainty.

"He could not recollect ever having made such a promise."

— Searching the memory and finding nothing — a very natural use.

These are ready-made phrases you will frequently see "recollect" appear in:

  • "as far as I can recollect" — meaning: to the best of my memory
  • "I don't recollect" — meaning: I don't remember (often implying some searching)
  • "if I recollect correctly" — meaning: if my memory is right
  • "I vaguely recollect" — a partial, uncertain memory
  • "try to recollect" — an explicit effort to remember

Be careful not to confuse recollect (one word, no hyphen) with re-collect (hyphenated).

  • Recollect = to remember
  • Re-collect = to collect something again (for example, "They had to re-collect the scattered papers.")

The hyphen makes all the difference. In almost all everyday usage, when you see "recollect" written as a single word without a hyphen, it means to remember.

Recollect means to deliberately and consciously bring a memory back to mind — to search your memory and retrieve something from the past. It emphasizes the active, often effortful nature of the act of remembering. It is slightly more formal and reflective in tone than everyday "remember," and it is especially at home when the memory is distant, uncertain, or requires some careful thought to retrieve.
13403: A recollection is a memory — something from the past that exists in your mind. It is the mental image, feeling, or awareness of something that happened before, which you are able to bring back into your thoughts. When you close your eyes and remember the face of an old friend, the smell of your grandmother's cooking, or the day something important happened to you — what you are accessing is a recollection.
The Three Senses of the Word

"Recollection" as a noun is used in three closely related ways, and understanding all three will give you complete mastery of the word.

The first and most common sense: a specific memory. Here, a recollection is one particular thing you remember — a moment, an event, a person, a detail from your past. It is a concrete piece of the past that lives in your mind.

"She had a vivid recollection of the afternoon her father taught her to swim."
"His earliest recollection was of a small, sunlit room with yellow curtains."
"I have no recollection of signing that document."

In this sense, "recollection" is a countable noun — meaning you can have a recollection, or many recollections.

The second sense: the act of remembering. "Recollection" can also describe the process itself — the mental effort of going back into your mind and retrieving something from the past. Think of it as the action of searching through your memories.

"The soldier's recollection of events grew difficult as the years passed."
"With careful recollection, she was able to describe exactly what she had seen."

The third sense: the general ability or capacity to remember. This is used to describe how well someone can remember things — how reliable or sharp their memory is in a given situation. You will almost always see this in one particular phrase: "to the best of my recollection."

"To the best of my recollection, the party was on a Friday night."
"That conversation, to the best of my recollection, never took place."

This phrase is extremely common and important to know. It signals that you are sharing what you remember as honestly as you can, while acknowledging that your memory may not be perfect.
The Key Quality That Sets "Recollection" Apart: Effort

This is one of the most important things to understand about this word. A recollection is not something that simply floats into your mind on its own. It implies a degree of active, conscious effort — the deliberate act of reaching into the past and pulling something forward. You try to recollect. You make an attempt.

This is what separates it subtly from the more general word "memory." A memory can just arrive — a song plays and suddenly you are flooded with memories of a past summer, without trying. But a recollection more often suggests you are making an effort to retrieve something. A witness on a stand trying to piece together what they saw. A grandparent carefully thinking back to describe how things were decades ago. Someone trying hard to remember whether they locked the door.

The difference is small but real: memory can be passive, while recollection carries a sense of mental effort and retrieval.

"Recollection" is a moderately formal word. It sits comfortably in professional, legal, literary, and academic contexts — a lawyer asking a witness about their recollection of events, a historian describing someone's written recollections of a war, an author reflecting on recollections of childhood. In everyday casual conversation, people more often say "memory" or "remember," but "recollection" is by no means rare or stiff in normal writing and speech. It simply sounds a little more considered and precise.
How It Compares to Similar Words

Since you will encounter these words alongside "recollection," knowing how they differ will sharpen your understanding.

Memory is the broadest of these words. It covers everything — the general ability to remember, the act of remembering, and individual things remembered. It is also the most neutral and common.

Recollection is more specific. It tends to emphasize the retrieval effort and is often used when the act of remembering requires some deliberate mental work.

Recall (as a noun) emphasizes speed and accuracy of retrieval — "She had perfect recall of every date in the textbook." It is the most clinical of the group.

Reminiscence is warmer and more personal. It describes the act of fondly or gently thinking back on the past, often in conversation or storytelling — usually pleasant, nostalgic memories shared with others.

Remembrance is the most solemn and formal. It is used for the act of honoring or commemorating something or someone — like Remembrance Day for fallen soldiers.

"to the best of my recollection" — as far as I can remember; this is my honest best attempt to recall. Used frequently in formal settings like legal testimony, and in everyday life when you want to be careful and honest about your memory.

"have a recollection of" — to remember something. "Do you have any recollection of what was said?"

"no recollection of" — to not remember something at all. "He had no recollection of the argument."

"a dim/hazy recollection" — a vague, unclear memory. "I have a dim recollection of visiting that town as a child."

"a vivid/clear recollection" — a sharp, detailed memory. "She had a vivid recollection of exactly what he was wearing."

"earliest recollection" — the first thing someone can remember from their life. "My earliest recollection is of sitting on my father's shoulders at a parade."

"Recollection" is a noun that captures the human experience of reaching into the past with your mind. It is a memory — specific and retrievable — brought forward through conscious effort. It is more precise and deliberate than the broad word "memory," and it carries a tone of thoughtfulness and care. Whether it is a witness trying to recall a face, a writer gathering memories of a distant childhood, or a friend saying "to the best of my recollection, that is how it happened" — this word is always about the careful act of retrieving the past and holding it up to the light of the present.
13404:
When you recommend something to someone, you are telling them: "I think this is good, and I think you should choose it or try it."

It combines two things at once — a positive judgment (you think it's good) and a direction (you're steering someone toward it). You are not just saying something is good in general; you are specifically saying it would be good for this person, in this situation.

"I recommend this restaurant."
= I have reason to believe it's good, and I think you specifically should go there.

When you recommend something, it's not random. There is always a basis for your recommendation — your personal experience, your knowledge, your expertise, or your research. This is what gives the word its weight.

It also implies goodwill — you want the other person to benefit. You are not being neutral. You are actively pointing them in a direction you believe is right for them.

This is why the word feels authoritative. A doctor who recommends a treatment is speaking from knowledge. A friend who recommends a book has read it and thinks it suits you. A critic who recommends a film has seen it and believes it's worth your time.

Suggest is the closest word, but it is softer and more tentative. When you suggest something, you are putting an idea on the table — you are less certain it's the right choice. When you recommend, you are more confident and more committed to your opinion.

"You could suggest taking the highway" → casual, uncertain.
"A mechanic recommends changing your oil every 5,000 km" → confident, based on expertise.

Advise is more formal and serious. It's often used by professionals (lawyers, doctors, financial advisors) when giving guidance in high-stakes situations. Recommend can be used both formally and casually.

Endorse is stronger and more public. You endorse something when you give it your official, public stamp of approval — often for products, candidates, or causes. Recommend is more personal and conversational.

Propose simply means to put forward an idea for consideration. It doesn't carry the positive judgment that recommend does.
Grammar: How to Use "Recommend" in a Sentence

This verb has specific patterns. Using the wrong one is one of the most common mistakes learners make.

Pattern 1: recommend + noun (a thing or person)

"I recommend this book."
"She recommended a good dentist."
"They recommended the chicken dish."

Pattern 2: recommend + gerund (-ing form of a verb)

"I recommend reading this book."
"Doctors recommend getting eight hours of sleep."
"He recommended taking the train."

⚠️ You cannot say "I recommend to read this book." In English, after recommend, you use the -ing form, not the to + verb form.

Pattern 3: recommend + that + subject + verb

"I recommend that you see a doctor."
"The report recommends that the company hire more staff."
"She recommended that he apply early."

Note: In formal writing, the verb after that is often in the base form (without -s, even for he/she/it):

"I recommend that he apply" (not applies)
"She recommends that the board reconsider" (not reconsiders)

This is called the subjunctive mood, and it's standard in formal English with recommend.

Pattern 4: recommend + object + to someone

"I recommend this hotel to all my friends."
"Can you recommend a good book to me?"
"She recommended the new doctor to her family."

⚠️ Another very common mistake: do not say "I recommend you to do this." English does not allow recommend + person + to + verb. Use Pattern 2 or Pattern 3 instead.

❌ "I recommend you to read this."
✅ "I recommend reading this." / "I recommend that you read this."

Everyday, casual situations:

"What do you recommend on the menu?"
"A friend recommended this series — I think you'd love it."
"I highly recommend the massage therapist at that clinic."

Professional and expert contexts:

"The doctor recommended complete rest for two weeks."
"Our financial advisor recommends diversifying your investments."
"The lawyer recommended settling out of court."

Formal and institutional contexts:

"The committee recommends approving the proposal."
"The World Health Organization recommends vaccines for all age groups."
"The report recommends stricter environmental regulations."

Recommending a person (for a job, award, opportunity):

"I would strongly recommend her for this position."
"His professor recommended him for the scholarship."
"Can you recommend someone for the job?"

Here, you are vouching for a person — saying they are suitable or capable.

Recommend is very commonly used in the passive voice, especially in instructions, guidelines, and formal writing.

"It is recommended that you save your work frequently."
"This exercise is recommended for people with back pain."
"Eight glasses of water per day are recommended by nutritionists."
"The use of sunscreen is strongly recommended."

The passive form makes the recommendation sound more general and objective — as if it comes from a broader authority rather than one specific person.

You can modify recommend to show how strongly you feel:

  • "I would recommend..." → polite, slightly hedged
  • "I recommend..." → direct, confident
  • "I strongly recommend..." → very confident, almost urgent
  • "I highly recommend..." → enthusiastic, very positive
  • "I do not recommend..." / "I wouldn't recommend..." → negative recommendation (caution or warning)

"I would not recommend driving in that area at night."
"I highly recommend this course to anyone interested in photography."
The Full Picture in One Place

To recommend (verb) means to tell someone — based on your knowledge, experience, or judgment — that a particular thing, person, or action is good, suitable, or worth choosing. It expresses both a positive assessment and a direction: you are actively guiding someone toward something you believe will benefit them.

It is more confident than suggest, less formal than advise in most contexts, and more personal than endorse. It can be used in everyday conversation and in formal, official writing. Grammatically, it is followed by a noun, a gerund (-ing), or a that-clause — never by to + verb directly after a person.

That, in full, is what recommend means and how it works.
13405:
A recommendation is a statement in which someone tells another person that something — a product, a person, a place, a course of action — is good, suitable, or worth choosing.

When you make a recommendation, you are essentially saying: "I think this is a good choice for you. You should consider it."

A recommendation has three key elements:

  1. A recommender — the person or body giving the suggestion.
  2. A recipient — the person who receives the suggestion and may act on it.
  3. The thing being endorsed — what is being suggested as good or appropriate.

Crucially, a recommendation is not a command or an order. The person receiving it is free to accept or reject it. It is a guided suggestion, not a requirement.

Understanding what a recommendation is not helps you understand it more sharply.

  • Opinion vs. Recommendation: An opinion is simply what you think or feel ("I think this movie is great"). A recommendation goes one step further — it is an opinion that also urges someone to take an action ("I think you should watch this movie"). All recommendations contain an opinion, but not all opinions are recommendations.
  • Advice vs. Recommendation: Advice is general guidance about what to do in a situation ("You should eat healthier"). A recommendation is more specific and often more formal — it points to a particular choice ("I recommend this brand of oats"). In practice, the two words overlap a lot, but a recommendation tends to be more direct and definitive.
  • Request vs. Recommendation: A request asks you to do something for the speaker. A recommendation suggests what you should do for your own benefit.
  • Instruction vs. Recommendation: An instruction tells you exactly what to do and often implies you must follow it. A recommendation is advisory — it guides but does not compel.

A recommendation carries the credibility and trust of the person giving it. When a doctor recommends a medicine, a teacher recommends a book, or a trusted friend recommends a restaurant, the advice carries weight because the recommender has relevant knowledge, experience, or authority.

This is why a recommendation from an expert or a trusted person feels more valuable than a random suggestion. The stronger the recommender's credibility, the more seriously the recommendation is taken.

Recommendations appear in many areas of life:

1. Informal, everyday recommendations
These happen in conversation between friends, family, or colleagues.

  • "You should try that new café on the corner — the coffee is excellent."
  • "I highly recommend this book. It changed how I think about habits."

2. Professional recommendations
These come from experts in a field — doctors, lawyers, financial advisors, consultants — who use their knowledge to guide a client's decision.

  • A doctor might say: "My recommendation is to rest for two weeks and avoid strenuous activity."
  • A financial advisor might recommend a particular investment strategy.

3. Formal written recommendations (Letters of Recommendation)
This is a very specific and common use of the word. A letter of recommendation (also called a reference letter) is a formal document in which someone — usually a teacher, employer, or mentor — writes about another person's qualities, abilities, and character, and endorses them for a job, a university, a scholarship, or an award.

In this context, "recommendation" means: I am officially vouching for this person's suitability.

4. Official / institutional recommendations
Governments, health organizations, and scientific bodies issue official recommendations based on research and expertise.

  • The World Health Organization issues health recommendations.
  • A government might issue dietary recommendations for its citizens.
  • A court might make a sentencing recommendation.

These carry authority and are taken very seriously, though individuals and institutions are still free to follow or ignore them.

5. Algorithmic / technology recommendations
In the modern world, recommendation also refers to the suggestions made by software systems.

  • When YouTube suggests a video, or Amazon suggests a product, or Spotify suggests a song, these are called recommendations.
  • The system behind this is called a recommendation engine or recommendation algorithm.

"Recommendation" can appear as singular or plural.

  • Recommendation — one specific suggestion.

"The doctor gave me a recommendation to see a specialist."

  • Recommendations — a set of suggestions, often at the end of a report or study.

"The committee's recommendations were submitted to the board."

In formal reports, business documents, or research papers, a dedicated section titled "Recommendations" is common. It contains the writer's proposed actions based on the findings of the report.

• To make a recommendation — to suggest something.

"Can you make a recommendation for a good hotel in Delhi?"

  • To follow a recommendation — to do what was suggested.

"She followed her doctor's recommendation and started exercising daily."

  • To act on a recommendation — to take action based on the suggestion.

"The company acted on the consultant's recommendations immediately."

  • On the recommendation of someone — because someone suggested it.

"He was hired on the recommendation of the senior manager."

  • A strong recommendation — a very firm or enthusiastic endorsement.

"She gave him a strong recommendation for the position."

  • A recommendation letter / letter of recommendation — a formal written endorsement of a person.
  • At someone's recommendation — the same as "on the recommendation of."

"At her teacher's recommendation, she applied to the advanced program."

A recommendation is a suggestion or endorsement that tells someone a particular choice, action, person, or thing is good, suitable, or worth pursuing. It comes from someone with knowledge, experience, or authority. It is advisory — not binding — meaning the recipient can choose whether to follow it. It appears in everyday conversation, professional contexts, formal letters, official reports, and digital technology.

The heart of the word is this: someone who knows better, or has experienced something, is pointing you toward what they believe is the right or best choice.
13406:
Recompense is something given to a person to make up for — or to acknowledge — a loss, harm, effort, or service they have experienced or provided.

The heart of the word is the idea of restoring balance. Something happened that created an imbalance: maybe you were wronged, maybe you suffered a loss, maybe you worked hard, maybe you did someone a great favor. Recompense is whatever is given in response to right that imbalance — to say, in effect, "this is what you are owed."

It can take many forms: money, an action, an apology backed by effort, a gift, a privilege, or anything else of value. What matters is not the form it takes, but the reason it is given — it is always given because something happened that made it deserved or appropriate.

The word is used in two closely related but slightly different situations:

1. To compensate for harm, loss, or suffering

This is when someone has been hurt, wronged, or has lost something, and recompense is what is given to make up for it. The giver is usually the one responsible for the harm, or someone acting on their behalf.

  • The factory polluted the river and destroyed the fishing community's livelihood. The court ordered the company to pay recompense to every family affected.
  • She lost her luggage due to the airline's negligence. The recompense she received — a voucher and a small sum of money — felt inadequate for the stress she had endured.
  • He had spread a false rumor about her, damaging her reputation. A public apology was the only recompense he could offer.

Here, recompense carries a sense of justice — it is what a wronged person deserves.

2. To reward effort, service, or a good deed

This is when someone has done something valuable — worked hard, helped generously, provided a service — and recompense is what they receive in acknowledgment of that. Here it overlaps with the idea of a reward or fair payment.

  • After twenty years of loyal service to the organization, her recompense came in the form of a generous pension and a heartfelt ceremony in her honor.
  • He fixed her car on a rainy night without being asked. She insisted on giving him something as recompense, but he refused to accept it.
  • The artist spent three months painting the mural for free. The city's recognition of her work in the local news felt like a small but meaningful recompense.

Here, recompense carries a sense of fairness — it is what a deserving person earns.

Both senses share the same fundamental logic: something is owed, and recompense is the fulfillment of that owing.

You will very often see the phrase "in recompense for" followed by whatever action or situation prompted it. This phrasing makes the connection between cause and response crystal clear:

  • She was given a scholarship in recompense for the opportunity she had been wrongly denied.
  • He cooked her a meal every week in recompense for her help during his illness.

This phrase is worth memorizing because it captures the word's essence perfectly: recompense is always for something.

Recompense is a formal word. You would encounter it in serious writing — legal documents, literature, formal speeches, journalism, and careful essays. In everyday casual conversation, people tend to say things like "make it up to you," "pay you back," "compensate you," or "give you something for your trouble" instead.

This doesn't mean the word is rare — you will encounter it fairly often in formal reading. But if you use it in casual speech, it will sound elevated and deliberate, which can sometimes be appropriate for emphasis or gravity.
How It Differs from Similar Words

Several words are close to recompense in meaning, but each has its own flavor:

Compensation is the closest synonym and is often interchangeable with recompense. However, compensation tends to feel more cold, technical, and transactional — it is the word you would expect in an insurance form, a legal settlement, or an HR document. Recompense carries a slightly warmer, more personal, and more morally weighted tone. "She received compensation" sounds like a procedure was completed; "she received recompense" sounds like justice was done.

Reward is used only for positive actions — you reward someone for doing well, not for suffering a loss. Recompense covers both harm suffered and good done, so it is the broader word.

Reparation is specifically about making amends for serious past wrongs, and it is most commonly used on a large, often political or historical scale — reparations for slavery, reparations for war damage. Recompense is used at both personal and large scales and doesn't carry that same heavy historical weight.

Remuneration refers specifically and narrowly to money paid for work or services. Recompense is broader — it is not limited to money, not limited to work, and includes suffering or loss as reasons for it.

Amends (as in "making amends") is closely related but tends to focus on the moral or emotional repair of a relationship — fixing what went wrong between people. Recompense is more tangible and outcome-focused — it is the actual thing given, not just the act of trying to repair things.

It is worth being clear about what the word does not mean:

  • It is not a random gift. A gift given out of affection with no reason of debt or service behind it is not recompense. Recompense is always prompted by something — a wrong, a loss, an effort, a service.
  • It is not an apology by itself. An apology might accompany recompense, but words alone, without any tangible or meaningful act of making things right, don't qualify. Recompense has substance to it.
  • It is not necessarily money. People often associate compensation with money, but recompense can be anything of value — time, effort, recognition, a privilege, an action.

Whenever you see or hear the word recompense, ask yourself: What happened, and what was given in response to it? The answer to "what was given in response" is the recompense. It is always the response to something, never random, and always carries the implication that it is deserved or appropriate — not just a nice gesture, but something owed.

It is, at its soul, the word for what fairness looks like in action.
13407:
To recompense someone means to give them something of value to make up for a loss, harm, or effort they experienced because of you or on your behalf.

Think of it this way: imagine a scale. On one side, something happened that was costly to a person — they lost something, suffered something, or gave something up. The scale is now unbalanced. To recompense them is to put something on the other side of the scale to restore the balance and make things fair again.
The Two Main Situations Where You Use It

Recompense covers two closely related situations:

1. Making up for harm or loss
When someone suffers a loss or damage — and you are responsible (or simply in a position to fix it) — you recompense them to make things right. The goal is to restore them, as closely as possible, to the position they were in before the harm happened.

The airline recompensed the passengers for the cancelled flight by refunding their tickets and covering their hotel costs.

The government recompensed the families who lost their homes when the dam burst.

2. Rewarding or paying back someone for their effort, sacrifice, or service
When someone gives their time, energy, or resources for your benefit, recompensing them means acknowledging what they gave and paying them back appropriately.

The general recompensed his soldiers for their years of loyal and dangerous service.

She was never fully recompensed for the hard work she put into building the company from nothing.

This is the most important thing to understand about recompense compared to simpler words like "pay" or "give."

Recompense always carries a moral weight. It implies:

  • That something is genuinely owed
  • That there is a debt — not necessarily in the financial sense, but in the moral sense
  • That the person receiving the recompense has a legitimate claim to it — they are not being given a gift out of generosity alone, but rather being given something that justice demands they receive

When you recompense someone, you are essentially saying: "What happened to you (or what you did) created an obligation, and I am now fulfilling that obligation."

This is why the word feels more serious and formal than just saying "pay" or "reward." There is always an underlying idea of righting a wrong or settling a moral account.
How It Compares to Similar Words

Understanding how recompense sits among similar words will sharpen your understanding considerably.

Reimburse — This is specifically about returning money that someone already spent. If your company pays for a work trip from your own pocket and your employer gives you that money back, they reimburse you. Recompense is broader — the "something of value" given doesn't have to match exactly what was lost; it just has to be sufficient to make things right.

Compensate — Very close to recompense in meaning, and often interchangeable. Compensate, however, tends to feel more clinical, legal, and transactional. Recompense carries a more literary, formal, and morally loaded tone. You'd see "compensate" in a legal contract; you're more likely to see "recompense" in a novel, a speech, or a formal written document.

Reward — Reward leans positive. You reward someone for doing something good. Recompense is more neutral — it applies equally to making up for something bad and acknowledging someone's effort or sacrifice. Also, a reward is often a voluntary extra; recompense is something that is owed.

Repay — Repay is most naturally about returning something specific (usually money or a favour) to its original owner. Recompense is broader and has a stronger moral implication of fairness.

The most natural way to use recompense as a verb is:

Recompense + [person] + for + [the loss/effort/harm]

The company recompensed him for his injuries.
She was recompensed for her years of unpaid work.
Nothing could truly recompense them for what they had endured.

You can also use it without the "for" part when the context already makes the reason clear:

They promised to recompense him, but never did.
The Register: When Do People Use This Word?

Recompense is a formal and somewhat literary word. You won't typically hear it in casual everyday conversation. It appears most naturally in:

  • Formal writing (legal documents, official letters, formal essays)
  • Literature and serious non-fiction
  • Speeches or contexts where elevated language is appropriate
  • Historical or journalistic writing

In everyday speech, people are more likely to say "compensate," "pay back," or "make it up to someone." But if you are reading a novel, a historical text, a legal opinion, or a formal letter and encounter this word, you now know exactly what it means and why it was chosen — the writer wanted to convey not just payment, but the moral weight of a debt being settled.

Here is a simple test to remember the word's essence:

Whenever you see or want to use recompense, ask: "Is something being given back or made right because fairness and justice demand it?" If yes, recompense is the right word. It is never a casual, purely spontaneous gift — it is always an answer to an imbalance that needed to be corrected.
13408:
"Reconcile" means to bring two things that are in conflict, separated, or out of agreement back into harmony. The two things could be people, ideas, feelings, or numbers. Think of it as making peace between things that don't currently fit together.

It has four distinct but closely related meanings.
Meaning 1: To restore a broken relationship between people

When two people have had a fight, a falling out, or a long separation, and they come back together and make peace, they reconcile.

"After years of not speaking, the brothers finally reconciled."
"She tried to reconcile her parents after their divorce."

Notice it works in two ways. When the people themselves make peace with each other, neither needs an object — they simply reconcile. But when a third person steps in to bring two conflicting people together, that person reconciles them.

The key idea: a rift existed, and now it has been healed.
Meaning 2: To make two things compatible or consistent with each other

This is the most intellectually rich use of the word. When you have two facts, ideas, beliefs, or statements that seem to contradict each other, and you find a way to show they can both be true — or you struggle because they simply can't be — you are trying to reconcile them.

"It's difficult to reconcile his generous donations with his history of cheating people."
"Scientists are working to reconcile the two conflicting theories."
"How do you reconcile your belief in fairness with this unfair rule you're enforcing?"

This use almost always appears as "reconcile X with Y" — meaning: make X and Y fit together consistently.

When you say "I can't reconcile these two things," you mean they appear contradictory and you cannot find a way to make them both true at the same time.
Meaning 3: To accept something difficult (reconcile yourself to something)

When someone accepts a reality they don't like — not happily, but with a sense of "okay, I have to live with this" — we say they have reconciled themselves to that reality.

"After losing the competition, she reconciled herself to the fact that she wasn't going to win this year."
"He slowly reconciled himself to living alone."

This meaning is always used with a reflexive pronoun — reconcile yourself, himself, herself, themselves — followed by "to" and the unwanted reality.

The emotional texture here is important: it's a quiet, reluctant acceptance. Not joy, but a hard-won peace with what cannot be changed.
Meaning 4: To make two sets of records agree (finance/accounting)

In financial and administrative contexts, "reconcile" means to compare two records and make sure they match — or to find and fix the differences between them.

"Every month, the accountant reconciles the company's bank statements with its internal records."
"Please reconcile your expense report with your receipts."

The logic is the same as always: two things that should agree are being brought into agreement.
The thread that ties every meaning together

In every single use of this word, the story is the same:

Two things were apart, inconsistent, or in conflict. Now they are being brought together.

Two people who fought are brought back together — relationship reconciled. Two ideas that clash are shown to be compatible — ideas reconciled. A person and an unwanted reality reach a point of acceptance — yourself reconciled to it. Two sets of records that don't match are made to agree — accounts reconciled.

Once you see this common thread, the word clicks permanently.

Reconcile with — to make peace or achieve consistency with someone or something. "She reconciled with her sister." / "He reconciled his beliefs with the new evidence."

Reconcile yourself to — to accept something difficult. "Reconcile yourself to the fact that things won't always go your way."

Hard/difficult/impossible to reconcile — used when two things seem deeply contradictory. "It's hard to reconcile his public image with his private behavior."

Irreconcilable — the adjective form, meaning "impossible to reconcile; so deeply opposed that no harmony is achievable." "They had irreconcilable differences" — you have likely seen this phrase in the context of divorce.
Three things that trip up learners

"Reconcile" is not the same as "forgive." Forgiving someone is about letting go of anger inside yourself — it can happen even without ever speaking to that person again. Reconciling means you've actually come back together and restored the relationship. You can forgive without reconciling, and in rare, unhealthy cases, people may technically reconcile without truly forgiving.

"Reconcile" is not the same as "compromise." Compromising means both sides give something up to meet in the middle. Reconciling means bringing two things into harmony — this might or might not involve compromise. The focus of reconcile is on the end state of harmony, not on what was surrendered to get there.

"Reconcile yourself to" does not mean you're happy about something. It specifically signals the acceptance of something unwanted or painful. You would never say "I reconciled myself to winning the lottery" — because that isn't hard to accept. The phrase only makes sense when the reality being accepted is difficult.
13409:
When something is reconciled, it means a state of peace has been reached after conflict, tension, or disagreement. The fighting — whether between people, within your own mind, or between two opposing ideas — has settled down. What was once at odds is now at rest.

Think of it this way: before reconciliation, something was broken, clashing, or unacceptable. After reconciliation, it has been accepted, healed, or brought into harmony. The adjective "reconciled" describes that resulting peaceful state.

1. Reconciled with a person (or group)

When two people or groups who were estranged, hurt, or in conflict have made up, forgiven each other, and restored their relationship, they are described as reconciled.

"After years of not speaking, the reconciled brothers finally sat down for a meal together."

"The reconciled nations signed a formal peace agreement."

Here, "reconciled" tells you the rupture in the relationship has been mended. There was a before — full of bitterness or distance — and now there is an after, where peace has been restored. The relationship isn't just paused or on hold; it has genuinely been repaired.

Important nuance: Being reconciled with someone usually involves forgiveness and mutual understanding. It is not merely a forced truce. It carries warmth and genuine restoration.

2. Reconciled to a situation (personal acceptance)

This is when a person has accepted something difficult, painful, or unchangeable — even if they don't fully like it. They've stopped internally fighting or resisting it. They've found a kind of peace with it.

"She was reconciled to the fact that she would never get her old job back."

"After months of struggle, he was finally reconciled to living with his illness."

Notice the word "to" here. You are reconciled to a situation, not with it, when it's something you're personally coming to terms with.

Key nuance: Being reconciled to something does not mean you are happy about it or that you approve of it. It simply means the internal war you were waging against the reality of it has ended. You've accepted what is, even if it still causes you sadness. Think of it as: "I've made peace with this, even though it hurts."

This is slightly different from being simply "okay" with something. Reconciled carries the weight of a real struggle that finally found rest.

3. Reconciled (two opposing things brought into harmony)

Sometimes "reconciled" describes two ideas, beliefs, facts, or pieces of information that seemed contradictory or in conflict but have now been made consistent and compatible with each other.

"His reconciled beliefs allowed him to be both a devoted scientist and a deeply spiritual person."

"The reconciled accounts showed the company's finances were completely in order."

In this use, "reconciled" tells you that something which appeared to clash now fits together cleanly. The contradiction has been resolved.

What separates "reconciled" from simpler words like "accepted" or "okay with" is the implied history of conflict. "Reconciled" always quietly announces: there was a problem before this. A rift, a disagreement, an internal resistance, a contradiction. The word carries that backstory in it.

This is why "reconciled" feels weightier and more meaningful than just saying someone "accepted" something or two people "made up." It signals that real friction existed, and real effort — emotional or otherwise — went into reaching this state of peace.

Being reconciled doesn't always mean completely at peace or joyful. Think of it on a spectrum:

  • At its warmest, reconciliation is full forgiveness, love restored, and genuine comfort with a situation.
  • At its quieter end, it's a calm resignation — no more internal fighting, even if there's still some sadness underneath.

Both ends are "reconciled." The word covers this whole range.

ContextExample
With a person"The reconciled couple left the therapist's office holding hands."
With a group"The reconciled political parties formed a unity government."
To a situation"He was reconciled to spending his retirement in a small town."
To a loss"She was reconciled to never knowing the full truth."
Two ideas/things"A reconciled theory brought together both schools of thought."
Finances/data"The reconciled figures confirmed there were no errors in the records."

• It does not mean pretending something never happened.
  • It does not mean being indifferent or numb. Reconciled people can still feel the weight of what they've been through.
  • It does not mean forced or fake peace. True reconciliation has depth and sincerity to it.
  • Being reconciled to a bad situation does not mean you think it was good or right. It just means you're no longer fighting what cannot be changed.
Reconciled describes a state in which conflict, tension, or resistance — between people, within a person's mind, or between opposing ideas — has found genuine peace and rest.
